newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ATPC urges U.S. to use restraint in tin sales.
newsitem.headline: ATPC urges U.S. to use restraint in tin sales.

text.p: The Association of Tin Producing Countries (ATPC) urged the United States on Tuesday to exercise restraint in its tin sales and complained about the lack of transparency in Washington's tin disposal programme.

"The conference noted with concern the announcement by the United States government of its latest plan for the sales of surplus tin," a joint statement issued by the ATPC at the close of its two-day conference in Singapore said.

"The (ATPC) would wish to reiterate its call on the government of the United States to respond positively to the approaches made by producers and to exercise restraint in her tin disposal programme," the statement said.

The United States has approved the sale of metals from the U.S. military stockpile to make up for an estimated $415 million shortfall in revenue from military sales fees of hardware sold to other countries running to the year 2005.

Washington said the sales, including tin, would not disrupt the metals market. The latest sale was announced by the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) on Monday when it sold 405 tonnes of stockpile tin to three bidders at $2.71 a lb.

The U.S. said in July it would offer up to 5,000 tonnes of tin in August for sale in long-term contracts which would be awarded in September. A further 5,000 tonnes would be offered in February and July, 1997.

Beginning with the new fiscal year in October, the United States will also offer a maximum of 200 tonnes on the first Tuesday of each month through sealed bids until the remaining 2,000 tonnes of sales authorised for the year is exhausted.
The use of long-term sales and monthly auctions "would mean there would be no transparency in tin sales by the DLA and producers would have difficulties in monitoring such sales," the ATPC said.
"The impact of those kind of sales on the price of metals like tin would be negative," a Singapore-based metal trader said. "It will affect the kind of price the producers may get."

The ATPC said tin exports by its members in 1995 were 100,023 tonnes, 10 percent higher than quotas set for the year. The higher exports were caused mainly by Indonesia, whose output was 48,000 tonnes against a quota of around 30,000 tonnes, delegates to the conference said. Production in 1994 was about 40,000 tonnes.

The ATPC said Brazil, currently an observer in the group, had reiterated its desire to become a member of the organisation. A senior Brazilian official said last week it is delaying membership because it would be "useless" to join a weak ATPC.
On its internal affairs, ATPC said an export quota system violated by many of its members would remain suspended for another year.

A Chinese official said on Monday Beijing favoured continuing the so-called supply rationalisation scheme (SRS), but Indonesia maintained that the free market system now in place worked best for the industry.
"It's obsolete," an Indonesian official said of the SRS.
Metal traders in Singapore said the system should be abandoned because nobody follows it anyway.

The ATPC accepted the decision by Thailand and Australia to leave the organisation. It said Australia would cease to be a member on December 10 while Thailand will leave the group on December 30, 1996.
The members of the ATPC are Bolivia, China, Indonesia, Malaysia and Nigeria. Zaire, which produces no tin, has stopped attending the meetings although it is still considered a member.
The next ATPC ministerial meeting will be held in Nigeria in September, 1997.
